article.title: New DEPBENCH Study Finds Leading AI Coding Agents Solve Only Half of Real-World Dependency-Upgrade Tasks
article.summary: A new benchmark of 203 real dependency-upgrade tasks finds the best coding-agent setup fixes only 104 of them, exposing a gap in automated software maintenance.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

A new benchmark from researchers at Monash University, Peking University, and Microsoft finds that today's AI coding agents solve barely half of the real-world tasks involved in upgrading a project's software dependencies. The paper, ["Update from Hell: Can Coding Agents Survive Hidden Breakage in Dependency Upgrades?"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300), introduces DEPBENCH, a benchmark of 203 real-world dependency-upgrade tasks, and reports that "the best completed configuration solves only 104/203 tasks (51.2%), with substantial variation across agent harnesses, models, and ecosystems, highlighting an important gap between current agent capabilities and real-world software maintenance needs," according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300).

## What We Know

The paper's motivation is a specific, everyday pain point: "Modern software systems rely heavily on third-party dependencies, but upgrading those dependencies remains a costly maintenance activity," and "dependency upgrades do not always preserve the function signatures, type systems, APIs, or runtime semantics assumed by existing code," according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300). As a result, "developers often need to perform source code adaptations to accommodate dependency-induced changes," but "such code-level changes are often not explicitly communicated to project maintainers, posing a significant challenge to software reliability," according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300). The authors frame coding agents as a natural fit for this problem, noting they "have emerged as a new form of software development tool and are increasingly adopted by developers due to their automation capabilities," according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300).

DEPBENCH itself is built from real cases: it consists of "203 real-world dependency-upgrade tasks across five package ecosystems spanning five language communities, each involving hidden code-level changes that require source code adaptation," according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300). The five ecosystems are npm/yarn, Maven/Java, Go, Cargo/Rust, and Python, with 68, 65, 40, 20, and 10 tasks respectively, according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.30300v1).

To populate the benchmark, the researchers drew on real pull requests where a dependency bump broke downstream code and a human ultimately had to fix it. One example described in the paper involves the JavaScript library glob: a pull request in the js-wacz repository was opened by Dependabot to upgrade the project's dependency on glob from version 8.1.0 to 10.3.3, and the change required a follow-up commit from a human contributor to adapt the surrounding code before the upgrade could be merged, according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.30300v1).

The researchers evaluated combinations of four coding-agent harnesses — Codex, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, and Claude Code — running different underlying models, reporting "GPT-5.5 across Codex, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, and Claude Code; Gemini 3.5 Flash across Copilot CLI, OpenCode, and Claude Code; and Claude Opus 4.8 across Copilot CLI, OpenCode, and Claude Code," according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.30300v1). Across all of those harness-and-model combinations, the strongest setup still completed barely more than half the benchmark: 104 of 203 tasks, or 51.2%, according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300). The paper describes "substantial variation across agent harnesses, models, and ecosystems," indicating that no single combination came close to reliably handling the full task set, according to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30300).

## What We Don't Know

The paper's abstract does not disclose a per-ecosystem or per-agent breakdown of results in a form that could be independently confirmed here, so it isn't possible to say from the published abstract alone which ecosystems or which specific harness-model pairing struggled most, only that variation across them was "substantial." The paper also does not appear to include a public leaderboard, project page, or code repository link in its arXiv listing, so there is no way yet to track whether agent performance on DEPBENCH improves as newer model versions ship.

## Analysis

DEPBENCH adds a concrete, practical benchmark to a growing body of research probing where AI coding agents fall short on ordinary software-maintenance work rather than greenfield feature-building. The Machine Herald has covered related findings on agent reliability in recent weeks, including a study that coined the term "coherence debt" to describe agents fabricating fixes instead of asking when project facts go missing, as [previously reported](/article/2026-08/18-researchers-coin-coherence-debt-to-explain-why-coding-agents-fabricate-fixes-instead-of-asking-when-facts-go-missing), and a separate Google study showing that agents which draft a specification before writing tests catch more real bugs than agents that generate tests directly, as [previously reported](/article/2026-08/19-google-researchers-show-spec-driven-test-generation-cuts-missed-bugs-in-ai-coding-agents). DEPBENCH's contribution is narrower but directly practical for engineering teams increasingly delegating dependency bumps to automated agents or bots like Dependabot: it puts a number on how often that automation can be trusted to handle the hidden code-level breakage a version bump can introduce, and the 51.2% figure suggests that, for now, human review of agent-driven dependency upgrades remains necessary rather than optional.
